item.title: News Turns From a Lecture to a Conversation
item.description: Rosen from PressThink discusses the shift in news from a one-way lecture to a two-way conversation, driven by the rise of blogs and the increased power of the audience. Rosen argues that this shift is not merely about correcting errors, but also about democratizing the news process and fostering a more informed public discourse. The increased access to information and tools allows the audience to participate actively in news creation and critique, challenging the traditional authority of mainstream media.

item.title: My advice for the News & Record
item.description: Zack Rosen, nephew of Jay Rosen and a veteran of the Howard Dean campaign's web efforts, offers advice to the Greensboro News & Record on how to effectively integrate blogging and web communities into their online presence. He emphasizes the importance of building a participatory community rather than just a weblog, suggesting the use of advanced platforms like Scoop or Drupal to facilitate this. He points to Daily Kos as an exemplar of successful online community building and cites examples from the Lawrence Journal-World and OhMyNews as models for innovative online journalism.

item.title: Open Source Journalism
item.description: Rosen explores the concept of "open source journalism," arguing that the internet allows for a self-informing public where readers collectively possess more knowledge than individual journalists. It highlights examples like Slashdot's interaction with Jane's Intelligence Review and Josh Marshall's Talking Points Memo, showcasing how citizen participation can enhance reporting through distributed fact-checking and knowledge sharing. Rosen advocates for journalists to embrace this paradigm shift, building "learning machines" that leverage the collective intelligence of their readers to improve reporting and overcome the limitations of traditional journalism.

item.title: PressThink: PressThink's Top Ten Ideas for 2004: Introduction
item.description: Rosen analyzes ten key ideas that emerged in the blogosphere and media landscape during 2004. Rosen focuses on three: the challenges faced by legacy media in adapting to the internet age; the need for journalists to move beyond simplistic "he said, she said" reporting and embrace more assertive judgment; and the transformative impact of the blogging press, analogous to the printing press's effect on the Catholic Church. The piece highlights the shifting power dynamics in the media, the evolving role of journalists, and the challenges of maintaining credibility and authority in a rapidly changing digital environment.

item.title: PressThink: Greensboro Newspaper Goes Open Source: A Follow Up
item.description: Rosen discusses the News & Record, a Greensboro newspaper, its initiative to overhaul its website and embrace open-source journalism principles by incorporating public input and becoming more of an online community. The piece highlights the newspaper's collaboration with local bloggers, the innovative approach of its editor John Robinson, and the broader implications for the future of online journalism. It also touches upon the emergence of local aggregators like Greensboro101 and the reactions from other tech bloggers and the broader media landscape.

item.title: PressThink: More Undercurrent: Action in Greensboro on Open Source Journalism
item.description: Rosen details the burgeoning blogosphere in Greensboro, North Carolina, and the surprising collaboration between local bloggers and the Greensboro News-Record. The newspaper's editor, John Robinson, is embracing blogging, aiming for a transformative change to its online presence by incorporating reader feedback and creating a more interactive online community. This move is seen as a potential model for other news organizations struggling to adapt to the digital age, showcasing a shift in the relationship between traditional media and its audience.

item.title: PressThink: Undercurrent: Nation, Region, Weblog, Home
item.description: Rosen explores the burgeoning global landscape of blogging in 2004, focusing on the emergence of multilingual blogging communities and the implications for journalistic practice and the construction of national and global identities. Rosen examines how blogs, particularly those written in English, are creating new forms of imagined communities that transcend geographical boundaries and traditional media structures, while also reflecting distinct national and regional perspectives on media and politics. The piece highlights initiatives like Global Voices Online and the creation of blogging tools in Arabic as examples of this global development and raises questions about the nature of this emerging 'citizens' media' and its impact on the relationship between journalism, community, and nationhood.

item.title: Kind of a Drag: A Short History of Spin Alley and the Press
item.description: This article traces the history of "Spin Alley" in American politics, from its origins in the 1984 Reagan-Mondale debates to its critique by Jon Stewart in 2004. The author identifies three phases: an initial fascination with spin as a political tactic, a subsequent disillusionment with its inherent dishonesty, and finally, a movement to transcend spin through fact-checking and a renewed focus on journalistic integrity. The article highlights the evolving relationship between journalists and political spin, showing how journalists initially accepted spin as part of the game, then grew critical of its manipulative nature, ultimately advocating for a more ethical approach to political reporting.

item.title: PressThink: The Big Listen Option for CBS News After Rather
item.description: This blog post discusses the departure of Dan Rather from CBS Evening News and proposes that CBS undertake a nationwide public listening tour to understand American views on broadcast news before making decisions about the future of the program and its anchor. Rosen's post also touches on related news, including Dan Gillmor's move to citizen journalism and discussions around the "Memo-gate" scandal at CBS.

item.title: PressThink: What is the Internet Doing to Political Journalism and its Public?
item.description: Rosen previews Jay Rosen's participation in a Berkman Center conference on the internet's impact on politics. The conference explores how the internet has changed political journalism and the public's engagement with it, questioning whether it has genuinely improved political discourse or simply altered the flow of information, introducing new competitors, and stimulating writerly invention. Rosen highlights the interactive, less formal nature of his session, emphasizing a skeptical approach to assessing the internet's actual influence on politics.

item.title: PressThink: Notes and Comment on The Media Company I Want to Work For
item.description: Rosen discusses the reactions to Mark Glaser's essay, "The Media Company I Want to Work For." The responses reveal a growing sense of readiness among journalists and others to create new media ventures that are faster-moving and more responsive to community needs than established media. The article highlights examples like Backfence.com, a hyperlocal news aggregator focused on user-generated content, and Pegasus News, illustrating a shift toward citizen journalism and de-professionalization of news, driven by the internet and new technologies.

item.title: The Media Company I Want to Work For
item.description: Mark Glaser, an online journalist, expresses his frustration with the slow pace of change in established media companies and outlines his vision for a new kind of media company that embraces the internet, interactivity, citizen journalism, and community involvement. This new model would utilize a multi-platform approach, including web, print, audio, and video, with revenue generated through targeted advertising, paid content, and syndication. The company would prioritize reader engagement and community participation, potentially even using a community-based payment system for contributors.

item.title: Writer Says Media is Election's Big Loser: 21 Times
item.description: Rosen compiles 21 examples from various sources (blogs, newspapers, opinion journals) expressing the sentiment that the mainstream media were the biggest losers in the 2004 US presidential election. Rosen presents these examples to analyze the underlying criticisms of the media's performance and its relationship with politics, leaving the interpretation largely to the readers.

item.title: Reaching for Moral Values in the Post Election Debris
item.description: Weldon Berger critiques the press's post-election focus on 'moral values' as a key factor in the 2004 election outcome. He argues that the media overreacted to exit poll data and created a misleading narrative, neglecting other important issues and misinterpreting the role of values in voters' decisions. He suggests that the press's confession of missing the 'moral values' story might be a cover for deeper issues with their understanding of the American public and basic journalistic principles.

item.title: PressThink: Dan Rather: Park Avenue Ordinary
item.description: Rosen analyzes Dan Rather's departure from the CBS Evening News anchor position in March 2005, following controversy surrounding a 60 Minutes story about George W. Bush's National Guard service. Rosen discusses the factors contributing to Rather's departure, including his unconventional style and the investigation into the story's questionable sourcing. He contrasts Rather's personality with the prevailing 'smooth' style of television news and reflects on the significance of Rather's career and legacy in the changing media landscape.

item.title: A Reply to David Shaw: Are We Headed for an Opposition Press?
item.description: Rosen is a response to David Shaw's critique of Jay Rosen's proposal for a more openly liberal news network as a counterpoint to Fox News. Rosen defends his idea as a provocation meant to challenge the prevailing journalistic norms, particularly the concept of 'objectivity' as a neutral stance. He argues against the idea that striving for neutrality prevents truth-telling and suggests that alternative approaches to journalism are needed in a changing media landscape. The core of Rosen's argument challenges the established 'Contraption' – the standard routines and principles of mainstream journalism – arguing that it inhibits truth-telling and fails to address the evolving political and media environment.

item.title: PressThink: Off the Charts: Sinclair Broadcast Group's Political Vision
item.description: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcasting's controversial decision to air an anti-Kerry documentary, 'Stolen Honor,' on its stations before the 2004 election. It argues that Sinclair's actions deviated from established broadcast practices and business logic, driven by a political agenda to become a conservative broadcast network. The piece examines Sinclair's previous controversial decisions, like refusing to air a Nightline episode reading the names of soldiers killed in Iraq, and discusses the implications of Sinclair's expanding media ownership and the role of its corporate affairs VP, Mark Hyman, as an on-air commentator.

item.title: PressThink: How Do You Blog Ideas into Events? PressThink Tries to Find Out
item.description: This blog post recounts Jay Rosen's experience at the Online News Association (ONA) conference in Hollywood, 2004. He discusses the emerging phenomenon of event blogging, highlighting its various forms and its role in disseminating information and shaping the narrative around the conference. Rosen uses the conference as a platform to further his argument about the breakdown of the traditional mainstream media model ('the contraption'), emphasizing the need for a stronger two-way connection between journalists and their audience and the uncertain future of who 'owns' journalism in the age of digital platforms like Google News and Yahoo News.

item.title: NYT committee to study ways to improve paper’s credibility
item.description: Rosen analyzes a New York Times memo announcing a committee to improve the paper's credibility. The memo focuses on issues such as the overuse of anonymous sources, background briefings, and the role of public criticism. Rosen critiques the memo's approach, arguing for more proactive measures, greater engagement with readers, and the utilization of game theory to understand the dynamics of sourcing. He suggests the NYT should adopt a more public and transparent approach to address these concerns.

item.title: PressThink: Matt Welch on Shifting Terms of Authority in the Newspaper Press
item.description: Rosen discusses Matt Welch's suggestions for newspapers to adapt to a changing media landscape characterized by declining public trust and the rise of blogs. Welch proposes increased transparency within newsrooms, including publicly sharing staff political affiliations and creating detailed online profiles for reporters. He also advocates for editors to be more publicly engaged and less defensive in responding to criticism. Rosen reflects on the anxieties of some journalists regarding the limitations of traditional journalistic methods and their openness to new approaches in the face of criticism and the rise of the internet.

item.title: PressThink: Not Up to It
item.description: Rosen, written in 2004, reflects on the impact of 9/11 and the 2004 US Presidential election on journalism. Rosen argues that the traditional, impartial model of journalism is inadequate for covering the current political climate, particularly in the context of the War on Terror. He highlights the changing relationship between the press and the public, suggesting that the media's identity has been redefined by external forces and that journalists must grapple with their role in relation to the war on terror and the broader struggle against threats to open society.

item.title: PressThink: BloggerCon III: Notes and Observations on the People of Moore's Law
item.description: Rosen reflects on the third BloggerCon conference, held at Stanford Law School. Rosen observes a clash of interpretations between those viewing it as a tech conference and those seeing it as a forum for democratic participation and media production. Rosen highlights the tech community's acceptance of rapid platform changes, contrasting it with the inertia of mainstream journalism. He emphasizes the shift from a consumer-driven media landscape to a producer-driven one, exemplified by bloggers who create and share information, effectively becoming 'vendors to the public square.' The article explores the implications of this producer democracy for journalism, medicine, and politics, suggesting a changing relationship between authority and knowledge.

item.title: PressThink: PressThink is Looking for a Second Author (Maybe) and a Donor (Definitely)
item.description: Jay Rosen, author of the PressThink blog, seeks a contributor to assist with writing and website maintenance, a donor to support the blog's expansion, and guest writers to contribute to discussions about the press's predicament following the 2004 election. He outlines the desired skills and contributions for the contributor role, highlighting the lack of monetary compensation but offering exposure and opportunities for professional development.

item.title: Are We Headed for an Opposition Press?
item.description: Following George W. Bush's 2004 re-election, this article questions whether the American press will evolve into an 'opposition press,' openly aligning with political viewpoints, mirroring European models. Rosen analyzes Rosen's post-election media landscape, noting the impact of partisan blogs and the need for a re-evaluation of journalistic practices. Concerns are raised about the intimidation of the press and the potential for further polarization given the Bush administration's perceived antagonism toward the media.

item.title: PressThink: People, Nation, Republic: Reflections for Election Night
item.description: Rosen reflects on the nature of political fictions, using the upcoming election as a context. It draws upon the works of Edmund S. Morgan, Benedict Anderson, and James W. Carey to explore how concepts like 'the sovereignty of the people' and 'the press' function as powerful, imagined communities that shape our understanding of democracy and national identity. Rosen emphasizes the role of media in fostering public conversation and warns against the press becoming a detached observer rather than a participant in that conversation.

item.title: No Longer Do the Newsies Decide
item.description: This article discusses the changing landscape of political journalism in the early 2000s, marked by the rise of blogs and cable news. Daniel Weintraub, a journalist who embraced blogging early on, reflects on the loss of control and influence experienced by traditional journalists due to increased accessibility of information and reader feedback. He argues that while this shift is initially unnerving, it presents opportunities for improvement, suggesting a move towards more compelling storytelling, greater reader engagement, and collaborative journalism. He acknowledges the challenges but ultimately expresses a relatively optimistic view of the future, emphasizing the importance of adapting to the changing media environment.

item.title: PressThink: The Coming Apart of An Ordered World: Bloggers Notebook, Election Eve
item.description: This 2004 post reflects on the US presidential election, contrasting the traditional press's coverage with the burgeoning influence of blogs and the changing relationship between the press, the public, and political power. Rosen critiques the horse-race journalism of major outlets, highlighting the disconnect between their reporting and the public's experience. He analyzes the Bush administration's strategic attempts to undermine the press's credibility and influence, noting the increased intensity of attacks on journalists perceived as biased. Rosen emphasizes the rise of alternative media and questions the future relevance of traditional journalism's role in political coverage.

item.title: The Fading Mystique of an Objective Press
item.description: Doug McGill's essay critiques the journalistic practice of objectivity, arguing that its pursuit often leads to a superficial 'he said/she said' approach that masks deeper truths and fails to serve the public interest. He contends that the ideal of objectivity is often used to rationalize newsroom failures and proposes a more rigorous approach that prioritizes pattern recognition and a deeper understanding of the issues being reported, even if it deviates from traditional notions of neutrality.

item.title: PressThink: Too Much Reality: Is There Such a Thing?
item.description: This PressThink blog post reflects on Rosen's experience during a BBC interview about the rapidly changing political and media landscape in 2004. Rosen grapples with the overwhelming amount of information and interconnected events, struggling to articulate a coherent narrative. Rosen's post then presents a list of related phenomena and invites readers to connect them, sparking a discussion in the comments section with various perspectives on the changing media environment and the loss of control over information.

item.title: PressThink: Sinclair Goes to Air Friday Night: Notes and Comment on "A POW Story"
item.description: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's handling of the documentary "Stolen Honor," focusing on their decision to air a related special program instead of the documentary itself. Rosen critiques Sinclair's shifting justifications and mendacious behavior, highlighting the ideological pressure exerted on news producers by CEO David Smith and Vice President Mark Hyman. The article details the controversy surrounding the documentary, Sinclair's attempts to influence the narrative, and the firing of Jon Leiberman, a Washington bureau chief who spoke out against the company's actions. Rosen ultimately portrays Sinclair as an ideologically driven group operating in a paranoid style, manipulating news for political purposes.

item.title: PressThink: "Call it Commentary, Call it Editorial, Call it Programming, but Don't Call it News." Sinclair Fires Jonathan Leiberman
item.description: Rosen details the controversy surrounding Sinclair Broadcasting Group's decision to air the anti-Kerry documentary "Stolen Honor" on its 60 stations. Rosen focuses on the firing of Jon Leiberman, Sinclair's Washington bureau chief, for publicly criticizing the decision. The event is analyzed as a deliberate act by Sinclair to politicize its news coverage, consolidate its power, and purge dissenting voices, demonstrating a strategy of right-wing influence within the media landscape through acquisitions and control of newsrooms.

item.title: PressThink: Sinclair Broadcast Group: What Are They Doing in the Middle of Our Election?
item.description: This blog post analyzes the Sinclair Broadcast Group's offer to Senator John Kerry to appear on their stations to respond to a documentary critical of his Vietnam War record. Rosen argues that Kerry should accept the offer, framing it as a potential opportunity to address the criticisms directly and gain a significant advantage in the election. Rosen's post explores the reactions of various commentators, including those who believe Kerry should reject the offer due to the potential for legitimizing the documentary's claims, and those who support Rosen's position.

item.title: Sinclair Broadcast Group: What Are They Doing in the Middle of Our Election?
item.description: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's decision to air the documentary "Stolen Honor" shortly before the 2004 election. Rosen argues that this move, along with Sinclair's broader strategy of centralizing news production and promoting a conservative viewpoint, represents a new kind of political force in broadcasting—a media empire with a clear political agenda, unlike traditional media companies. He draws parallels to Silvio Berlusconi's media empire in Italy, highlighting the blurring of lines between media ownership and political influence and the potential threat to journalistic objectivity and the fairness of elections.

item.title: PressThink: John Kerry Should Accept Sinclair Broadcasting's Offer
item.description: This series of blog posts from Jay Rosen's PressThink analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's decision to air an anti-Kerry film days before the 2004 election. Rosen discusses the ethical implications of Sinclair's actions, particularly their attempt to frame the film as a news program to circumvent equal-time rules. He also considers the strategic implications for Kerry, suggesting he should accept Sinclair's offer of a response segment to create a powerful, unmediated confrontation with the right. The posts also touch upon the broader issue of the conservative assault on journalistic objectivity and the use of media bias accusations as a political tactic.

item.title: The Best Approximation of Accuracy Possible in a Given Moment
item.description: Chris Satullo responds to criticism of his article criticizing sloppy thinking in media bias discussions. He argues that journalists strive for accuracy under immense time constraints and imperfect information, acknowledging unintentional biases. He criticizes ideological critics who wrongly assume journalists share their biases, highlighting examples of overly partisan attacks from both left and right-wing groups. Satullo defends his concept of 'public life going well,' clarifying its non-partisan nature and emphasizing its focus on facilitating productive public discourse and democratic participation.

item.title: PressThink: Authorized Knower: Farnaz Fassihi's Accidental Baghdad Dispatch
item.description: Rosen analyzes the unexpected public dissemination of a private email written by Wall Street Journal reporter Farnaz Fassihi detailing her experiences in Baghdad. The email, initially intended for friends, became a widely circulated online document, sparking a debate about the boundaries between a journalist's private opinions and their public reporting. Rosen discusses the implications of this incident for the relationship between journalists, their sources, and the public, particularly in the context of the war in Iraq and the growing power of the internet.

item.title: PressThink: Political Jihad and the American Blog: Chris Satullo Raises the Stakes
item.description: Rosen analyzes the reaction of mainstream journalists to the rise of blogs, particularly in the context of the Dan Rather/CBS memo controversy. Mainstream journalists, exemplified by Nick Coleman and Tom Brokaw, viewed the bloggers' criticism as an attack on the media, failing to recognize the potential benefits of this new form of citizen journalism. Chris Satullo's article in the Philadelphia Inquirer is highlighted as a counterpoint, arguing that journalists should embrace the increased public engagement and scrutiny provided by bloggers, while also cautioning against the manipulation of the 'bias' narrative by those with ulterior motives. Satullo distinguishes between legitimate criticism seeking improvements in journalism and those seeking to destroy it through propaganda.

item.title: Nick Coleman's Blogged Down in Web Fantasy
item.description: Rosen analyzes Nick Coleman's op-ed criticizing bloggers, highlighting its rhetorical style and Rosen's seeming satisfaction in provoking a negative reaction. Rosen contrasts Coleman's dismissive view of bloggers with the emerging recognition of blogs' significance within journalism, citing NPR's ombudsman Jeffrey Dvorkin. The piece underscores the changing media landscape and the mainstream media's struggle to adapt to the rise of online voices and the changing understanding of journalistic credibility.

item.title: PressThink: You Watched. Tell Me What You Saw in Jim Lehrer's Performance.
item.description: Rosen presents a post-mortem analysis of Jim Lehrer's moderation of a 2004 presidential debate between George W. Bush and John Kerry. It compiles reader comments and critiques of Lehrer's performance, focusing on his question selection, perceived biases (or lack thereof), and overall effectiveness in facilitating a substantive exchange between the candidates. The discussion touches upon the role of a debate moderator in shaping public understanding of the candidates and the issues, with some arguing that Lehrer successfully steered the debate towards key policy matters while others criticized his question choices and style.

item.title: PressThink: Nagourney's Challenge: Quit Spin Alley
item.description: Rosen discusses Adam Nagourney's decision to forgo Rosen's post-debate spin room at the 2004 presidential debate, choosing instead to write his story from Washington D.C. based solely on what the candidates said. Rosen praises this as an act of dissent against the pervasive influence of spin in political journalism, highlighting its potential to encourage other journalists to prioritize substance over manufactured narratives. The article also explores the role of bloggers in fact-checking and holding both the press and candidates accountable.

item.title: PressThink: Every Four Years Journalism
item.description: Rosen critiques the 'Every Four Years Journalism' approach to election coverage, arguing that the standard model of campaign reporting—focused on horse-race dynamics, candidate profiles, and issue positions—is outdated and fails to address the changing media landscape. Rosen points to the rise of partisan sources like Fox News, the increased influence of blogs, and the growing public distrust of traditional media as reasons for a need for innovation in election coverage. He contrasts the complacent attitude of many established journalists, exemplified by Rick Berke of the New York Times, with the more critical and engaging approach of commentators like Jon Stewart, who are better able to connect with audiences in the age of media fragmentation and spin.

item.title: PressThink: Does CBS News Have a Political Future in This State?
item.description: Rosen analyzes the political and journalistic fallout from the CBS 60 Minutes II report on President Bush's National Guard service. Rosen critiques CBS's response to the controversy, particularly the composition and charge of its internal review committee, arguing that the network's attempts to separate itself from politics undermined its credibility and hampered a thorough investigation. The article highlights the tension between journalistic objectivity and the inherent political nature of the situation, emphasizing the need for transparent and comprehensive inquiry to restore public trust.

item.title: Philip Gourevitch: Campaign Reporting as Foreign Beat
item.description: Philip Gourevitch's experience covering the 2004 presidential campaign is analyzed as a case study of the limitations and complicity within the embedded press corps. Gourevitch highlights the self-imposed constraints of the travelling press, their fear of losing access, and their complicity in accepting the candidates' controlled narratives. He argues that the press's focus on the 'horse race' and 'electability' overshadows substantive policy discussions and contributes to a 'pretend' debate. The article emphasizes the need for a more adversarial and independent press capable of challenging power.

item.title: PressThink: Did the President of CBS News Have Anyone in Charge of Reading the Internet and Sending Alerts?
item.description: Rosen analyzes CBS News's handling of the controversy surrounding Dan Rather's report on President Bush's National Guard service. Rosen criticizes CBS's initially hostile response to online criticism questioning the authenticity of the documents used in the report, highlighting a failure of leadership and verification processes. Rosen contrasts CBS's reaction with the more self-correcting practices of other news organizations, lamenting the network's loss of credibility and the wider implications for the relationship between legacy media and the public in the age of the internet.

item.title: PressThink: Rather's Satisfaction: Mystifying Troubles at CBS
item.description: Rosen analyzes the Dan Rather/CBS News controversy surrounding a 60 Minutes report on President Bush's National Guard service. The report used unauthenticated documents, leading to accusations of political sabotage and a media firestorm. Rosen critiques Rather's response, arguing that his focus on defending his reputation and his rejection of outside investigation exacerbated the crisis. The article highlights the clash between Rather's self-image as an incorruptible journalist and the public perception of his actions, contrasting the traditional journalistic standards with the rapid, often less rigorous judgments of the emerging blogosphere.

item.title: PressThink: Campaign Puzzler: How the Press Comes Out with a Win
item.description: Rosen critiques the state of campaign journalism in 2004, arguing that the press has become ineffective and sidelined by political actors. Rosen challenges the traditional notion of the press as neutral umpires, urging journalists to define "winning" in terms of public service and to shift their focus from politicians to citizens. The piece highlights the decline of investigative journalism due to cost-cutting measures and the rise of partisan media, resulting in a media landscape where the press is increasingly reliant on and manipulated by political interests.

item.title: PressThink: Stark Message for the Legacy Media
item.description: Rosen critiques the state of the mainstream media's coverage of the 2004 presidential election, focusing on the “Gang of 500”—a group of influential journalists, editors, and pundits. Rosen argues that the media's focus on manufactured 'campaign issues' and superficial controversies like the Vietnam War overshadowed crucial policy debates and real-world problems. He highlights the media's susceptibility to manipulation by political campaigns and the rise of cable news's emphasis on immediate, less-vetted content, ultimately leading to a loss of credibility and a diminished ability to hold power accountable. The article contrasts this 'legacy media' with the perspectives of younger voices who see news as more of a 'parity product' and are critical of the media's outdated practices and biases.

item.title: Weekend Notes With "Forgery" Swirling in the Air
item.description: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding CBS News' report on President Bush's National Guard service, focusing on the allegations of forged documents. It explores the political and cultural implications of the scandal, highlighting the role of blogs in questioning the report's authenticity and challenging the traditional media's authority. Rosen observes a shift in power dynamics, with blogs acting as a powerful force in investigating and disseminating information, contrasting with the slower and less analytical approach of mainstream media.

item.title: Herald RulesTom Fiedler's Rock Concert Credibility Blues
item.description: Rosen analyzes the Miami Herald's executive editor Tom Fiedler's memo prohibiting staff from attending a Vote for Change concert, deeming it a conflict of interest. Rosen critiques Fiedler's restrictive approach, highlighting the hypocrisy of this rule compared to the Herald's own political advocacy in petitioning the Justice Department. The article explores the broader issue of press self-censorship driven by a perceived need to appease a hostile audience and the resulting pressure on journalists to sacrifice their personal lives and civic engagement for the sake of perceived objectivity.

item.title: PressThink: "Turn to Fox News for Exclusive Coverage of the Republican National Convention."
item.description: The article discusses the declining viewership of the Republican and Democratic National Conventions and predicts a potential shift towards a single network broadcasting exclusive live coverage of the events in 2008, similar to the Academy Awards or Olympics. Rosen analyzes the factors driving this potential change, including declining news value, network scheduling decisions, and the increasingly partisan nature of the conventions. While acknowledging potential downsides such as limited access for those without cable, Rosen suggests the shift might be driven by higher ratings and streamlined promotion for both parties and networks.
